title: Catherine of Genoa
hookLine: a noblewoman who ran a hospital and taught that purgatory is love's fire

cards: She was born into a powerful family of Genoa, and she spends her days changing bandages on a hospital ward. Under her apron, the cloth is fine. She also runs the place: the accounts, the supplies, the staff.
When sickness sweeps through Genoa, she stays. Years before, she was an unhappy young wife who could barely get out of bed.
Then something happened to her in a confessional, and it gave her an unexpected way of talking about purgatory.

teach.b: Start with the long dark stretch. Catherine was married young to Giuliano Adorno, and the marriage was unhappy; he was careless with money and with her. For years, the stories say, she lived in deep sadness.

teach.h: A CONFESSION, AND A FLOOD OF LOVE.
teach.b: Kneeling for confession, tradition says, she was overwhelmed by a sense of God's love so strong she could hardly speak. She left changed.
In time Giuliano changed too, and the two of them gave themselves to the sick at the Pammatone hospital in Genoa, where Catherine came to run the house.
In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says, "sick, and you visited me." Catherine took that at its word. Then, her teaching.

Her followers gathered what she said about purgatory, and her picture isn't a prison. The Catechism calls purgatory a final purification for those who die in God's grace but still need to be made clean.
Catherine describes it from the inside.
The soul sees God's love clearly and wants nothing else, and the fire it feels is that love burning away whatever still stands in between.

The souls there, she says, suffer and are glad at the same time, because they know where they're going. Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims, that such a person "shall be saved, yet so as by fire." Finally, her own life.
Some readers see her teaching written in it first: years of grief, then love burning through, leaving her free to wash other people's wounds.

how: Catholics pray for the dead, especially at Mass and in November, trusting that those being purified are helped by the prayers of the living; Catherine's writing on purgatory is still read as spiritual reading.

o: a prayer said for the dead on All Souls' Day
a final cleansing for souls already in God's grace
a place of punishment for souls God has rejected

games.q: Catherine of Genoa — tap the pairs.
p: the Genoa hospital she came to run
saved, yet so as by fire

s: Catherine pictured purgatory as a prison of punishment
she described its fire as God's love burning away what stands between the soul and God.
Catherine ran the hospital as well as nursing in it
she came to run the house at the Pammatone in Genoa.
Catherine of Genoa and Catherine of Siena are the same saint
two different women: Catherine of Siena urged the pope back to Rome; Catherine of Genoa nursed the sick and ran a hospital.

games.q: you're Catherine, from a powerful family, changed after years of sadness. what do you do with your life now?
o: return to society and enjoy your rank again.
go to work among the sick at the city hospital.
shut yourself away from everyone in a cell.
games.why: she and Giuliano gave themselves to the sick at the Pammatone, and she came to run it.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is ill or worn down, in a hospital, at home, maybe in your own house, and see them clearly, their room, their face.

Then choose one small thing you could do for them: a meal left at the door, a call, an hour sitting with them. If you pray, hold them before God or ask Catherine's prayers; if not, just hold them, and settle on the plan.

wordCard.voice: Purgatorium. The Church's name for the final purification of a soul already in God's grace, which Catherine of Genoa pictured as love's own burning. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the Church's name for the final purification of those who die in God's grace.

carryVoice: Your line: love burns clean. Grief wasn't the end of Catherine's story. Day eight hundred thirty-two.
